t.3.37.1: Thus was I then somehow spared by him in that battle. Now hear also what happened, what followed after that.
t.3.37.2: Though I had been treated in that way, I was not disheartened, and together with two rākṣasas who had taken the form of deer, I entered the Daṇḍaka forest.
t.3.37.3: With a blazing tongue, a huge body, sharp horns and great strength, I roamed the Daṇḍaka forest as a great flesh-eating beast.
t.3.37.4: At the fire-sacrifices, at the sacred fords, and beneath the shrine-trees, O Rāvaṇa, I roamed about, utterly terrible, assailing those ascetics.
t.3.37.5: Having slain in the Daṇḍaka forest the ascetics who walk the path of dharma, he drinks their blood and likewise devours their flesh.
t.3.37.6: Then, cruel and eating the flesh of sages, terrifying the creatures that roamed the forest, I wandered through the Daṇḍaka forest, intoxicated with blood.
t.3.37.7: Then I, a violator of dharma, roaming in the Daṇḍaka forest, came upon Rāma, an ascetic devoted to dharma.
t.3.37.9: Then I, recalling our former enmity and thinking, "This is a mere ascetic," disregarded the mighty Rāma who had gone to the forest.
t.3.37.8: the illustrious Vaidehī, Lakṣmaṇa the great chariot-warrior, and the ascetic who is restrained in his food and devoted to the welfare of all beings.
t.3.37.11: Having drawn his mighty bow forcefully, he loosed three sharp arrows, destroyers of foes, that flew like Suparṇa and the wind.
t.3.37.10: Remembering that blow, I rushed forward in great fury in the form of a sharp-horned deer, eager to kill, foolish as I was.
t.3.37.12: Those three arrows, like thunderbolts, most dreadful, feeders on blood, with well-bent joints, all came on together.
t.3.37.13: Knowing Rāma's prowess, and wily as one who had already seen danger before, I slipped away and so was freed, while those two rākṣasas were slain.
t.3.37.14: Hurled away by Rāma's arrow, I somehow escaped with my life, and here I have renounced the world; I am now an ascetic, disciplined and composed in mind.
t.3.37.15: Indeed, in every tree I see Rāma, clad in bark garments and black antelope skin, bow in hand, like Antaka, Death himself, holding his noose.
t.3.37.16: Stricken with fear, O Rāvaṇa, I see even thousands of Rāmas; this whole forest appears to me as if it had become Rāma.
t.3.37.17: Indeed, O lord of the rākṣasas, I see only Rāma wherever I am alone; and when I see Rāma come to me in my dreams, I start up, bereft of my senses.
t.3.37.18: O Rāvaṇa, since I am terrified of Rāma, names beginning with the syllable ra, and even jewels and chariots, fill me with dread.
t.3.37.20: If you do not heed these words, spoken to you as they are by me, who seek the welfare of my kinsman, then today, together with your kinsmen, you will lose your life in battle, slain by Rāma with his straight-flying arrows.
t.3.37.19: I know his might; a fight with him is not fitting for you. Either fight Rāma in battle or show forbearance, O Rākṣasa; but if you wish to see me, you must not speak of Rāma.
